After Rome took Egypt from Cleopatra in 30 BCE, merchant fleets began sailing each year from Red Sea ports such as Berenice and Myos Hormos straight across the open sea to India. A main goal was Muziris on the Malabar coast, the great pepper port.

The trick was the monsoon. Sailors left Egypt in midsummer and the southwest wind carried them across the Arabian Sea in a few weeks; the northeast winds of winter brought them home. Greek sailors had learned the pattern in the Ptolemaic period, but traffic grew sharply under Augustus; the geographer Strabo heard of some 120 ships a year sailing for India.

  • Westward went black pepper, pearls, ivory, fine cottons and gems.
  • Eastward went wine, olive oil, glass, coral and, above all, Roman gold and silver coins, found in hoards across south India.

A guidebook from the first century, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes the ports. Pliny the Elder grumbled that India drained the empire of money. The trade linked the Roman Empire to the Tamil kingdoms for over two centuries.
